topics.title: Chapter 8 — Booting Linux and systemd
topics.summary: HarborStatus works after an administrator starts it manually. After reboot, the host is reachable but the website is absent. The application was never connected to the machine’s startup lifecycle. Another service starts automatically but fails because its data mount is not ready. Startup is a dependency problem, not just a list of commands to run quickly.

blocks.text: HarborStatus works after an administrator starts it manually. After reboot, the host is reachable but the website is absent. The application was never connected to the machine’s startup lifecycle. Another service starts automatically but fails because its data mount is not ready. This chapter traces the boot path and shows how systemd represents units, ordering, activation, supervision, and failure. Its most important distinction is between a process being started and a service being ready to do useful work.

topics.title: 8.1 The Linux Boot Process
topics.summary: A conventional boot progresses through firmware, a boot manager or loader, the kernel, early user space, the real root filesystem, and the system’s main init process. Details vary with architecture, encryption, cloud images, and distribution tooling.

blocks.text: A conventional boot progresses through firmware, a boot manager or loader, the kernel, early user space, the real root filesystem, and the system’s main init process. Details vary with architecture, encryption, cloud images, and distribution tooling.

Each stage has different evidence. Firmware may fail before the kernel produces any log. An initramfs problem may prevent the real root filesystem from mounting. A systemd service failure occurs later, after the kernel and substantial user space are already working.

When diagnosing a boot failure, identify the last successful stage. “The server does not boot” is too broad to select a repair. A photo or console transcript of the exact error is often more useful than repeatedly power-cycling the machine.
Linux example — 8.1
Inspect the current boot and its timing.

systemd-analyze
journalctl -b -n 30 --no-pager
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Missing firmware timing may reflect the environment rather than a boot failure.

topics.title: 8.2 BIOS and UEFI

blocks.text: BIOS and UEFI are firmware interfaces that initialize hardware and select how to launch the operating system. UEFI commonly uses an EFI System Partition containing boot applications. Secure Boot can verify trusted components in that chain, subject to platform and distribution configuration.

A useful inspection is whether /sys/firmware/efi exists on a normally booted machine. This can help identify the current boot mode, but recovery procedures must still account for the installed bootloader and actual disk layout.

Do not switch firmware mode casually after installation. A system installed for one mode may not have the required files or boot entries for the other. Firmware settings, boot entries, and encryption recovery keys belong in the recovery plan, not only inside the guest’s filesystem backup.
Linux example — 8.2
Determine whether the current boot exposes EFI state.
if [ -d /sys/firmware/efi ]; then printf 'UEFI boot\n'; else printf 'EFI interface absent\n'; fi

blocks.text: GRUB is a commonly used bootloader that can select a kernel and supply its command line. Distribution tools often generate its configuration from templates and scripts. Editing the generated file directly can be overwritten by later updates.

Debian-family and RHEL-family systems differ in helper commands, configuration locations, and use of Boot Loader Specification entries. Follow the procedure for the installed release and boot mode rather than copying a generic grub-install command.

A temporary boot-menu edit can help test a kernel parameter without immediately making it persistent. Record exactly what changed and whether the next ordinary boot should retain it. A one-time rescue change is not a complete permanent fix.
Linux example — 8.3
Read GRUB's administrative defaults if present.
test -f /etc/default/grub && sed -n '1,80p' /etc/default/grub
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Reading defaults does not prove the generated bootloader configuration matches them.

topics.title: 8.4 Kernel Initialization

blocks.text: These inspect the running kernel’s state. The command line may contain infrastructure details, so review before sharing. Kernel messages can reveal missing devices or driver failures, but the earliest output may only be visible on the console if persistent logging never started.

A kernel panic is different from a later service failure. Preserve the error, kernel version, and recent changes. Booting a known-good installed kernel can be a recovery option when the distribution’s boot configuration and storage remain intact.

topics.title: 8.5 Initramfs
topics.summary: An initramfs is an initial filesystem used during early boot. It can contain drivers and tools needed to locate, unlock, assemble, and mount the real root filesystem. Encrypted storage, LVM, RAID, and network-root setups may depend on it.

blocks.text: An initramfs is an initial filesystem used during early boot. It can contain drivers and tools needed to locate, unlock, assemble, and mount the real root filesystem. Encrypted storage, LVM, RAID, and network-root setups may depend on it.

If a required storage driver or configuration is missing, the kernel may run but never reach the installed system. Rebuilding an initramfs can be appropriate after a verified cause, using tools such as dracut on RHEL-family systems or update-initramfs on Debian-family systems.

Do not rebuild blindly from an incorrectly mounted rescue environment. Confirm the target root, boot filesystem, kernel version, and required modules first. Otherwise you can create an image for the wrong system while believing the repair succeeded.
Linux example — 8.5
List initramfs artifacts and the running kernel.

uname -r
find /boot -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*initr*' -print
blocks.title: Original Linux example

blocks.text: What to check: Multiple artifacts may exist; identify the one matching the intended boot entry.

topics.title: 8.7 systemd Architecture
topics.summary: systemd represents managed resources as units and resolves activation relationships among them. It supervises processes through service units and cgroups, integrates logging with the journal, and supports sockets, mounts, timers, and targets.

concepts.definition: systemd represents managed resources as units and resolves activation relationships among them. It supervises processes through service units and cgroups, integrates logging with the journal, and supports sockets, mounts, timers, and targets.

blocks.text: systemd represents managed resources as units and resolves activation relationships among them. It supervises processes through service units and cgroups, integrates logging with the journal, and supports sockets, mounts, timers, and targets.

The system manager is distinct from a per-user manager. systemctl ordinarily addresses system units; systemctl --user addresses the current user’s manager. Configuration paths, permissions, and startup lifetime differ.

A useful mental model is desired lifecycle plus observed state. Unit files describe how a resource should be managed; systemctl asks the manager to act or report; logs explain what happened. Editing a unit file does not automatically start the service or reload its application configuration. (R17)
Linux example — 8.7
List active unit types and boot dependencies.

systemctl list-units --no-pager
systemctl list-dependencies default.target --no-pager

blocks.text: What to check: Loaded units are not the same as every installed unit file.

topics.title: 8.8 Units
topics.summary: A unit is a named object managed by systemd. The suffix identifies its type: .service, .socket, .timer, .mount, .target, and others. Different unit types describe different responsibilities.

blocks.text: A unit is a named object managed by systemd. The suffix identifies its type: .service, .socket, .timer, .mount, .target, and others. Different unit types describe different responsibilities.

Vendor units commonly live under /usr/lib/systemd/system or a distribution-equivalent path. Local system overrides belong under /etc/systemd/system. Use systemctl cat name.service to see the main file and drop-ins rather than assuming one visible file contains the complete effective configuration.

Prefer a drop-in for a narrow override. Replacing the entire vendor unit can prevent future package improvements from taking effect. Some list-valued settings require an empty assignment before replacement, so consult the setting’s documented merge behavior.
Linux example — 8.8
Inspect a target unit's definition and state.

systemctl cat multi-user.target
systemctl show multi-user.target -p LoadState -p ActiveState

topics.title: 8.9 Services
topics.summary: A service unit defines a process lifecycle: how to start, under which identity, with what environment and limits, and how to stop or restart. The Type= setting determines how systemd interprets startup.

cards.code:

systemctl show systemd-journald.service -p MainPID -p ActiveState
cards.answer: A service may be active while an application-level function still fails.

blocks.text: A service unit defines a process lifecycle: how to start, under which identity, with what environment and limits, and how to stop or restart. The Type= setting determines how systemd interprets startup.

Type=simple considers startup early in the launch process. Type=exec waits until the executable is invoked successfully, but still does not prove application readiness. Type=notify lets a cooperating program announce readiness. Type=oneshot is useful for a task that completes rather than running continuously.

A successful oneshot unit may become inactive after completion unless configured otherwise. That is not automatically failure. Select the service type that matches the actual program rather than forcing every task to look like a permanently running daemon. (R18)
Linux example — 8.9
Inspect a service without restarting it.

systemctl status systemd-journald.service --no-pager
systemctl show systemd-journald.service -p MainPID -p ActiveState

blocks.text: A target groups units and expresses a synchronization or activation point. multi-user.target commonly represents a non-graphical multiuser system, while graphical.target adds graphical-session requirements.
Targets are not simply old-style numeric runlevels with new names. Their relationships form a dependency graph, and multiple targets can be active at once.

topics.title: 8.11 Dependencies
topics.summary: Requirement dependencies and ordering dependencies are different. Wants= requests activation without the same failure coupling as Requires=. After= specifies ordering when relevant units are started; it does not by itself request their activation.

cards.answer: After controls ordering; it does not by itself pull a unit into the transaction.

blocks.text: Requirement dependencies and ordering dependencies are different. Wants= requests activation without the same failure coupling as Requires=. After= specifies ordering when relevant units are started; it does not by itself request their activation.

After=network.target does not mean the internet, DNS, or a remote database is reachable. network-online.target depends on the configured wait-online implementation and still is not a guarantee that a particular external service will remain available.

Applications need timeouts and retries for runtime dependencies. A correct boot order cannot prevent a database from failing later. Express necessary local mounts with supported dependency settings, and make application readiness explicit where the program provides a mechanism.

reading.title: 8.11 Dependencies
paragraphs: Requirement dependencies and ordering dependencies are different. Wants= requests activation without the same failure coupling as Requires=. After= specifies ordering when relevant units are started; it does not by itself request their activation.

After=network.target does not mean the internet, DNS, or a remote database is reachable. network-online.target depends on the configured wait-online implementation and still is not a guarantee that a particular external service will remain available.

Applications need timeouts and retries for runtime dependencies. A correct boot order cannot prevent a database from failing later. Express necessary local mounts with supported dependency settings, and make application readiness explicit where the program provides a mechanism.

blocks.text: This combines enablement and immediate startup. Use it only when both are intended. disable --now similarly combines future disablement with a current stop.

Disabling does not prevent all possible activation: another unit, socket, or manual request may start the service. Masking prevents ordinary activation by replacing the unit’s load path with a mask, but it can break dependencies. Use masks deliberately and document why a simple disable is insufficient.

blocks.text: A custom service should specify an absolute executable path, an appropriate identity, a lifecycle type, restart behavior, and necessary directories or limits. Do not depend on a personal shell’s aliases, current directory, or exported variables.

systemd does not interpret ExecStart= as an ordinary shell command line. Pipes, redirections, and shell built-ins require a deliberately invoked shell or, preferably, a separate reviewed script. Environment handling also differs from interactive Bash.

Validate with systemd-analyze verify and test actual startup. Hardening settings such as NoNewPrivileges=, PrivateTmp=, and ProtectSystem= can reduce access, but they can also expose undeclared application write requirements. Add restrictions with tests rather than copying the largest possible list. (R19)

topics.summary: The default target determines the normal activation goal at startup. Inspect it before changing it. A headless server often uses multi-user.target, but graphical or specialized systems can have other intentional arrangements.

blocks.text: The default target determines the normal activation goal at startup. Inspect it before changing it. A headless server often uses multi-user.target, but graphical or specialized systems can have other intentional arrangements.

Use systemctl list-dependencies to inspect relationships, recognizing that a textual listing is not a complete timing trace. systemd-analyze critical-chain can help explain startup ordering and delays, but parallel activity and service-readiness semantics still require interpretation.

A long boot can result from a missing mount, a device timeout, network wait-online behavior, or an application startup timeout. Reducing a timeout may hide a required dependency rather than solve the underlying problem. Identify what the system is waiting for.

blocks.text: Rescue and emergency environments provide reduced operation for recovery. Available services, mount state, authentication, and networking depend on the distribution and boot path. Do not assume remote SSH will remain available.

Use the hypervisor or physical console, and know where encryption and administrative recovery credentials are stored. A recovery shell may have the root filesystem mounted read-only. Remounting it writable is a deliberate step that should follow inspection of storage health.

Keep recovery activity minimal and recorded. A rescue environment is not an excuse to disable every protection permanently. Repair the identified configuration, validate it, and return through the normal boot path to prove that the repair is complete.

topics.title: Service configuration
topics.summary: Change — disposable VM. Install the root-owned executable, then create /etc/systemd/system/harbor-heartbeat.service with these contents:

blocks.text: Change — disposable VM. Install the root-owned executable, then create /etc/systemd/system/harbor-heartbeat.service with these contents:

[Unit]
Description=HarborWorks teaching heartbeat
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=exec
ExecStart=/usr/local/libexec/harbor-heartbeat
DynamicUser=yes
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3
TimeoutStopSec=10
NoNewPrivileges=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
